subject.note: Community-wide subject; listed named speakers are not a complete resident or ownership register.
subject.gist: Neighbors clustered adobe homes to preserve desert and share daily life, winning rezoning and later digging out their aging wastewater wetland together.

story.text: Milagro starts with neighbours who want company and room for the desert to remain desert. They persuade neighbours and the city to let them cluster adobe homes, with parking outside and porches facing one another. The walk home becomes a chance to catch up; children can run between houses, while back porches offer privacy. Their shade surprises even the founders: trees flourish on water reused from household drains through a shared treatment wetland. After twenty years, that wetland needs painstaking digging and gravel cleaning. This is a community where sharing daily life also means doing the work that keeps the place alive.

claims.text: Parking away from the houses makes residents walk, providing exercise and opportunities to meet people.

A resident uses the back porch for privacy and the front porch when wanting to socialize.
A resident reports living here for 23 years.
A resident moved from Wisconsin, having drawn communities as a child and fallen in love with the Sonoran Desert at age five.
Developing shaded areas was crucial because otherwise the community would be too hot.
Anyone can pick the community’s figs without asking permission.
Adobe was a breakthrough because the founders needed a house material they could afford that would work in the desert.
The adobe bricks were made locally in town and suited the desert.
Agreeing that everyone would have adobe walls, metal roofs and scored concrete floors helped bring the group together.
The founding household collects water in a cistern behind the porch screen and two more at the back.
Fitting solar on the founding couple’s roof was difficult, but a solution was found.
Most households preferred leaving the adobe exposed; one household covered it.
The founding home felt cool after the outdoor heat with no air conditioning running.
The founding home combines kitchen, dining and living rooms in a small space that feels airy and open rather than cramped.
Beth describes cohousing as people intentionally living together because they want to know their neighbors.

claims.text: Beth found her previous neighborhood isolating because her family knew only nearby neighbors and no children.
Beth’s family moved here when her daughter was nine years old.
Children can run between houses to find friends without residents worrying about cars.
The children organized their own community meal just for children in the shared kitchen.
Beth says there is enough for children to do here that parents can send them outside to play instead of spending time online.
Beth’s family saw the house for sale, and it felt like home when she walked in; she loved the deep porch.
Beth’s family did not want a large house and chose one of the smaller homes, which she estimates at 1,500 square feet.
Beth says the concrete floor stays cool and is warm in winter.
Beth describes passive solar design with deeper north-facing porches and more winter light on the south-facing side.
Beth attributes energy bills of about $25 a month to the combination of adobe and solar.
Beth says the house was built around a saguaro she tentatively estimates to be about 150 years old.
Beth agrees her house stays cool without air conditioning because of its thick adobe walls.
Beth’s living ocotillo fence has sprouted leaves and grown tall in places.
Beth’s family felt they did not need a larger house because there was so much shared space.
Beth and her husband both work from home, using the loft as an office and guest room.
Working parents shared school carpooling because many of their children attended the same school.
Residents own their individual houses while also having communal space.
Kitchen sinks and large windows face the path so residents can see people passing.
Vegetation gives Beth privacy while allowing her to stay connected with the community.
Outdoor gathering spaces mean Beth does not necessarily feel she has to invite people into her home.
Parties and porch pubs start on residents’ porches and spread into the shared gathering area with tables and food.
Planting uses layers of large mature trees, smaller trees underneath and shrubs.
A founder brought a mesquite from his Tucson backyard and planted it here in 2000; he calls it 20 years old.

claims.text: The transplanted mesquite thrived because of the community’s irrigation system.
The landscaped community began as barren land with nothing planted there.
The trees receive nitrogen and other nutrients from household effluent, including toilet wastewater.
Brad Lancaster helped the community arrange natural drainage and basins to collect rainwater.
Each house has a basin that holds rainwater while it soaks into the soil.
Household wastewater goes into septic tanks, where solids remain while the water continues to the wetland.
Sinks, toilets and showers supply the wetland with 2,000–3,000 gallons of water a day.
A resident says she had no idea what she was getting into with the desert water and planting systems.
A resident raised her children in the Midwest and moved to Tucson at age 44, later growing to love it.
The community owns 25 acres of desert wash.
Homes had to be above the 100-year flood level because summer monsoons cover almost the entire wash with flowing water.
The community chose not to develop another five acres high enough for building because it wanted to preserve the desert.
The founders wanted clustered homes to build community and retain desert rather than the area’s usual one house per three acres.
Household water enters underground through a distribution point that directs it to either the west or east wetland basin.
Water stays in the wetland for about three days while bacteria between the stones partly clean it.
The wetland’s bacteria arrive naturally in the household wastewater.
A buried perforated pipe distributes incoming water through the wetland for treatment.
An outlet pipe collects treated water and sends it through a box to the collection tank.
The collection-tank pump switches on when water reaches a set level and sends water back up into the community.
After 20 years, accumulated eroded soil and roots reduced the wetland’s performance, requiring rehabilitation.
Residents painstakingly dig out wetland rocks and screen away dirt because the clogged material no longer works as well.
A liner beneath the wetland bed holds the water in place.
The wetland gravel will be cleaned and put back into the bed.
The residents expect cleaning and erosion control to give the wetland another 20–30 years of service.
Reclaimed water is pumped underground to the top of the community and flows back down by gravity.
Gutters and downspouts route rain from both neighboring roofs into a tree’s basin.
Digging out the rainwater basin was hard work.
The land is shaped to direct water into depressions where it can soak in instead of running off the property.
A resident recalls the mulberry trees being laden with fruit the previous year.
claims.doubt: The caption calls the fruit “blackberries” immediately after identifying fruiting mulberry trees.

claims.text: The mulberries do well because they receive underground irrigation.
Residents’ daily sink and water use supplies 2,000 gallons a day to the underground irrigation.
The goal is 50 gallons per person per day, compared with the speaker’s Tucson estimate of about 110 gallons per person per day.
Some residents meet the water-use goal well and others do not; the speaker accepts this variation as part of community life.
Participating residents review their water bills every month to track how much they are using.
Fruit trees near residents’ houses are for the whole community, and anyone may pick from them.
Residents are attentive to native plants instead of bringing in trees such as pines.
The community owned its land but lacked road access, so it exchanged land with the school board to secure an entrance.
A founder says keeping a dream in mind and living it can bring the breaks they call miracles.
The description says 28 households have spent 28 years building the community.
claims.doubt: The description’s 28-year account differs from the film’s 1993 starting point; the periods described may be different.

claims.text: The design began with water rather than homes because the site is in a desert.
The description says the rain gardens and earthen basins let rain soak into the earth within 20 minutes of a storm.
The description says land outside the eight acres of housing is permanently preserved desert accessible to everyone.
The description credits shared meals, borrowed tools and supportive neighbors with making people stay.
Beth says the adobe walls also retain heat after the house is heated.
The wetland basin is “40 by 40” and receives 2,000–3,000 gallons daily, depending on household water use.
claims.doubt: The speaker gives no unit for the basin’s “40 by 40” dimensions.
